transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello Doctor. I came in because... gosh, I just feel like I cannot settle inside my own skin anymore. It's like this awful feeling where I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I am completely worn out and I really should just be sitting still. 

Like yesterday, I tried to just sit down and watch my stories—I've been watching *General Hospital* since I was in high school, and let me tell you, the storylines lately are just ridiculous. Sonny is always in some kind of trouble, I don't know how he gets away with it. But anyway, I couldn't even sit through a whole scene. I got up to fix a crooked picture frame in the hallway, and then I saw a smudge on the glass, which reminded me I needed to buy paper towels. The prices at the grocery store right now are just highway robbery, by the way. I went to get a carton of eggs last week and nearly had a heart attack right there in aisle four. The young man working the register didn't even know how to bag the groceries right, put my bread right under a giant bottle of laundry detergent. 

But yes, I just... I can't seem to stay sitting down, even when my bones are tired.

When you're trying to focus on something—like watching your show or reading—do you find it hard to keep your mind on it, or is it more that your body just needs to move even though your mind might be willing to sit still?

Well, it's... it's definitely my mind too, not just my tired old bones. I mean, I can sit down with the senior center newsletter—they mail it out every month, usually on a Tuesday, though last month it didn't come until Thursday because of the holiday. And don't get me started on the post office these days, I swear they lose half my mail. My niece sent me a birthday card with a check in it and it took three weeks to get here. Three weeks! 

But anyway, I'll sit down with the newsletter, or maybe the choir schedule for church, and I start out fine. I'm looking right at it. But then after just a few minutes, I realize my eyes have just been going over the same lines again and again, and I have absolutely no idea what I just read. It's like my brain just packs up and leaves the room. Just like that new choir director we have, he's always wandering off in the middle of practice to take a phone call. I don't know who he's talking to, but it's certainly not helping us learn the Easter cantata, I'll tell you that much.
Have you always had this trouble focusing and sitting still, even when you were younger—say, in school or as a young adult? Or is this something that's more recently started bothering you?

Oh, well... no, it's not new at all. Lord, I think I came out of the womb this way! Even back in grade school, I remember my teachers—Mrs. Higgins in third grade, she was a strict one, wore these awful horn-rimmed glasses and always smelled like mothballs and peppermint. She used to write on my report cards that I was a bright girl but just so careless. I was always losing my spelling papers or talking out of turn. 

I sat next to a boy named Tommy Jenkins, and Tommy was always bringing frogs to school in his pockets. Can you imagine? Just right there in his corduroys. One time, one got loose during a math test, and I was the one who got in trouble because I couldn't stop talking about it! Mrs. Higgins was always having to remind me to stay in my seat or finish my worksheets. I just couldn't sit still, not even then. 

And Tommy, well, he ended up moving away in the fifth grade, his father got a job at the Ford plant up in Detroit. I always wondered what happened to him. Probably still collecting frogs, if I had to guess. But yes, it's always been this way for me, losing things and needing to be told to just sit down and finish what I started.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity beginning in childhood (grade school), persisting into adulthood. Core symptoms include inability to sustain attention on tasks (reading newsletter, watching TV), constant need for movement despite fatigue, distractibility, carelessness with materials, and difficulty remaining seated. Symptoms cause functional impairment (cannot complete activities, loses items). No evidence of secondary medical or psychiatric cause. Presentation is consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Combined Type, Persistent into Adulthood (F90.9).
